<reason>A genuinely close, high-quality exchange. CON's case was built on a clever reframe ("nothing in hiring is necessary," so the motion is either a slogan or an override) plus a vacuum argument that removing degrees shifts weight to more wealth-wired interviews and referrals. CON extracted a real concession ("complied, if the review was honest") and its A1 on licensing/cheap-error jobs was the sharpest single answer in the debate. But PRO defended the motion as written more convincingly: it caught CON's quiet substitution of "improves odds at the margin" for "genuinely necessary," showed the interview is a constant rather than a substitute (so the degree is an extra gate, not the alternative to bias), and neutralized CON's named harm by noting the first-generation graduate keeps her diploma while her cousin gains a hearing. PRO also turned CON's own legal-shield history into evidence that the filter was never validated, and CON's own workable criterion in A1 (substitute standard exists or error is cheap) undercut its claim that "genuinely necessary" names nothing. CON's dilemma remained partly live, but PRO's norm analogy ("don't ask about age") and the wording-vs-screening distinction were adequate. PRO's triple clipping and mislabeled "C" references are real execution costs that keep the margin thin; CON's superior rhetoric does not overcome the fact that its harm case was largely dissolved.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's response to CON's vacuum/interview argument (B4.4–B4.5, B5.3): graduates are interviewed too, so the interview is a constant and the degree merely removes the poor candidate before gate two; and the graduate loses nothing under the motion while her cousin gains a hearing. CON's counter that the diploma is "the only part of the stack a stranger can acquire alone" was then cut down by PRO's observation that it is acquired with money and debt—CON's equity case depends on treating that toll as free.</best_rebuttal>
